questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman sought medical advice after being bitten on the leg by a stray coyote. She had received all appropriate travel immunizations 5 months previously for an overseas trip, including a course of rabies vaccine. The wound had been cleaned thoroughly. The animal could not be captured.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: 4 doses of rabies vaccine and rabies immune globulin (HRIG)
5 doses of rabies vaccine and rabies immune globulin (HRIG)
Obtain a rabies serologic titer from the patient

questions.explanation: 2 doses of rabies vaccine This patient who was previously vaccinated for rabies has now had a potential rabies exposure. She should receive two intramuscular doses of the vaccine. The first dose should be given immediately and a second dose 3 days later. The rabies immune globulin does not need to be given in this case because the woman was previously vaccinated. If she had never been vaccinated or had not received the full vaccine series, the rabies immune globulin would be indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q41

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl in Missouri was found asleep in a room with a bat. Her parents brought her to the clinic to assess the risk of rabies and to instigate management if required. She had not received rabies vaccinations prior to this.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Give 4 vaccines (d0, d3, d7, d14) plus rabies immunoglobulin
Give 5 rabies vaccines (d0, d3, d7, d14, d28)

questions.explanation: Give 4 vaccines (d0, d3, d7, d14) plus rabies immunoglobulin Bats are a potential source of rabies-related viruses. Bat bites are usually felt rather than seen. However, 50% of human cases with bat-variant rabies virus in the United States have resulted from unrecognized bat bites. Guidelines differ currently between the US and UK. ACIP guidance for the US in this situation advises 4 doses for postexposure prophylaxis and rabies immunoglobulin. Current Public Health England guidance is that where there is uncertain physical contact, such as with a young child, then treatment should be initiated with vaccine. If the patient is non- or partially immune, this should be with 4 doses. RIG (rabies immunoglobulin) is only additionally required for nonimmune patients in direct contact with bats, or patients who are immunosuppressed.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q6

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man seeks medical attention on returning from a camping holiday in Germany. He sustained a bite wound to his left hand 4 days previously from a wild fox he had tried to feed by hand. He has not seen any other healthcare professionals. He is concerned about the risk of rabies. He has received a full course of tetanus vaccinations and the wound looks clean and dry.

options.text: Five doses of IM rabies vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28
Human rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound

questions.explanation: Reassurance only Western Europe (including Germany) is free of rabies in terrestrial animals. As such, even though a bite that penetrates skin is high risk, the epidemiology means that rabies postexposure prophylaxis is not warranted. If this had been a bat bite, this would not be the case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q46

questions.question: For the following organisms, list the latest time that immunoglobulin can be given as post-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: For the following organisms, list the latest time that Ig can be given as PEP.

parts.text: Measles
Varicella-zoster virus
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis A
Rabies

parts_raw.text: Measles
VZV
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis A
Rabies

questions.model_answer: a) Measles: within 6 days of exposure (active vaccine if given within 72 hours). b) VZV: as soon as possible, up to 10 days after exposure. c) Hepatitis B: as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and up to 7 days after percutaneous/perinatal exposure (up to 14 days after sexual exposure). d) Hepatitis A: within 2 weeks (14 days) of exposure. e) Rabies: RIG given with the first vaccine dose; if not given then, it can still be administered through day 7 of the vaccine series.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rabies figure (RIG through day 7) is from this chapter; the measles, VZV, hepatitis B and hepatitis A immunoglobulin windows are from CDC/ACIP and PHAC immunization guidance, not the Mandell rabies chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Measles: 6 days (vaccine within 72 hrs). VZV: 96 hours – 10 days. Hepatitis B: 12 hours, up to 7 days for needle and infants, 14 days for sexual contact. Hepatitis A: 14 days. Rabies: up to Day 7 after vaccine given.

questions.question: Rabies virus.

parts.text: What are 4 routes of transmission?
What are 4 fluid/tissue samples (other than saliva) that should be collected pre-mortem (does not ask what tests to do on them)?
Why is sending a single saliva sample of limited sensitivity?
What is the classic finding on pathology?
Another person gets bitten by a wild rodent. Should you offer prophylaxis?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 routes of transmission
What are 4 fluid/tissue samples (other than saliva) that should be collected pre-mortem (doesn’t ask what tests to do on them)
Why is sending a single saliva sample of limited sensitivity?
What is the classic finding on pathology
Another person gets bit by a wild rodent. Should you offer prophylaxis? (0.5)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Animal bite with salivary contamination of a wound; (2) saliva contacting mucous membranes or non-intact skin; (3) inhalation of aerosolized virus (e.g., caves with heavy bat guano, laboratory exposure); (4) organ/tissue transplantation (solid organ, corneal) from an infected donor. b) (1) Full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy (nape of neck, above hairline); (2) serum; (3) CSF; (4) corneal impression/wash. c) Virus is shed intermittently in saliva, so a single specimen may miss it; antemortem diagnosis requires several specimens and multiple methods, and RT-PCR of saliva is reliable only if three successive samples are tested. d) Encephalitis with Negri bodies - eosinophilic cytoplasmic neuronal inclusions (concentrated in hippocampal pyramidal cells), with perivascular lymphocytic cuffing. e) Generally no. Small wild rodents are not a rabies reservoir and rarely transmit rabies; perform a risk assessment and consult public health - PEP is warranted only if the rodent's behavior was highly unusual.

cohort_answer.text: Routes: Saliva through bite/wound, saliva to mucus membrane or respiratory tract, organ transplant (SOT and corneal), aerosolized rabies (lab-acquired). Samples: Nuchal skin biopsy, Saliva, Serum, CSF, Corneal wash samples. Saliva sensitivity: positive late in disease. Pathology: Negri bodies (pathognomonic cytoplasmic inclusions), mononuclear infiltration, perivascular cuffing of lymphocytes/PMNs, lymphocytic foci. Wild rodent bite: depends on size; small rodents (mice, rats) unlikely to carry rabies as they usually die from the encounter

questions.question: You see a 14-year-old female who presents with fever, seizures, and altered level of consciousness. On examination you note hypersalivation, agitation, diffusely increased tone, and opisthotonic posturing. Her family notes she was bitten by a bat on her right hand approximately 4 months ago and did not seek medical attention.
questions.question_raw: You see a 14 year-old female patient who presents with fever, seizures, and altered level of consciousness. On examination, you note hypersalivation, agitation, increased tone diffuse, and opisthotonic posturing. Her family notes she was bitten by a bat in her right hand approximately 4 months ago. She did not seek medical attention.

parts.text: List TWO diagnostic tests that should be performed.
List TWO methods by which this infection can be transmitted in humans.
How should this patient have been managed at the time of her bite with respect to post-exposure prophylaxis?

parts_raw.text: List TWO diagnostic tests that should be performed.
List TWO methods this infection can be transmitted in humans.
How should this patient have been managed at the time of her bite with respect to post-exposure prophylaxis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Direct fluorescent antibody staining / RT-PCR of a full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy; (2) detection of rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies in serum and CSF (RFFIT), and/or RT-PCR of saliva. b) (1) Bite from a rabid animal with salivary contamination of the wound; (2) mucous-membrane or aerosol exposure to virus, or organ/corneal transplantation from an infected donor. c) Immediate thorough wound cleansing (20% soap solution +/- virucidal agent), then full post-exposure prophylaxis: HRIG 20 IU/kg with the entire dose infiltrated into/around the wound if feasible (remainder IM at a distant site), plus rabies vaccine 1.0 mL IM in the deltoid on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 (five doses if immunocompromised). Tetanus prophylaxis as indicated.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Animal bite with salivary contamination; (2) saliva contacting mucous membranes/non-intact skin; (3) aerosol inhalation (bat caves, laboratory); (4) organ or corneal transplantation from an infected donor. b) (1) Full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy; (2) serum; (3) CSF; (4) corneal impression/wash. c) Virus is shed intermittently in saliva, so a single sample can be falsely negative; diagnostic yield requires multiple successive samples (RT-PCR reliable if three successive saliva samples tested) and multiple methods. d) Negri bodies - eosinophilic cytoplasmic neuronal inclusions containing viral nucleocapsids. e) Generally no. Rats and other small rodents are essentially never found to be rabid; perform a risk assessment and consult public health - PEP is not routinely indicated.

questions.question: Rabies virus. A woman with a missed bat bite 6 months ago now has clinical rabies.

Q57 (2009 PM)
Rabies virus

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies in serum and CSF (RFFIT; CSF antibody is diagnostic even after PEP); (2) DFA staining and/or RT-PCR of a full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy (or RT-PCR of saliva). b) Immediate wound care plus full PEP: HRIG 20 IU/kg infiltrated into/around the wound (remainder IM at a distant site), given with the first vaccine dose (or up to day 7 of the series), plus rabies vaccine 1.0 mL IM in the deltoid on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 (add day 28 / five-dose schedule if immunocompromised).

cohort_answer.text:
A: CSF or serum for neutralizing anti-rabies antibodies (gold standard). Nuchal skin biopsy for DFA (direct fluorescent antibody)/PCR. Saliva for PCR. Serology. Brain biopsy

B: Rabies Ig day 0 (20 IU/kg given directed into wound site). Rabies vaccine day 0, 3, 7, 14, (28 if immunocompromised). + Tetanus ppx

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies in serum and CSF; (2) DFA/RT-PCR of a full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy (or saliva RT-PCR). b) (1) Bite from a rabid animal; (2) organ/corneal transplantation, or aerosol/mucous-membrane exposure. c) HRIG 20 IU/kg with the whole dose infiltrated into/around the wound if feasible (remainder IM at a distant site), given as soon as possible (with the first vaccine dose, or through day 7 of the series), PLUS rabies vaccine 1.0 mL IM in the deltoid (lateral thigh in small children, never gluteal) on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 - five-dose schedule (add day 28) if immunocompromised. d) Virus is shed intermittently in saliva, so a single sample may be negative; antemortem diagnosis needs several specimens and multiple testing methods. e) Encephalitis with Negri bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic neuronal inclusions), plus perivascular lymphocytic cuffing and mononuclear infiltration. f) Generally no - small wild rodents are essentially never rabid; do a risk assessment and consult public health, offering PEP only if the animal's behavior was highly unusual.

cohort_answer.text:
A: CSF or serum for neutralizing anti-rabies antibodies (gold standard). Nuchal skin biopsy for DFA/PCR. Saliva for PCR. Serology. Brain biopsy

B: Organ transplant. Animal bite. (Spelunking in cave with guano+++ airborne: rare) (Laboratory - airborne: rare). Skinning/handling infected carcasses

C: Rabies Ig day 0 (20 IU/kg given directed into wound site). Rabies vaccine day 0, 3, 7, 14, (28 if immunocompromised)

D: Intermittently shed in saliva, diagnostic yield higher with multiple sample

E: Histopathologic evidence of rabies encephalomyelitis (inflammation) in brain tissue and meninges includes: Mononuclear infiltration, Perivascular cuffing of lymphocytes or polymorphonuclear cells, Lymphocytic foci, Babes nodules consisting of glial cells, Negri bodies (neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions)

F: Need to conduct a risk assessment and consult public health. Generally in rodents, PEP only warranted if behavior of the biting animal was highly unusual

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with right shoulder pain, hypersalivation, and other symptoms of rabies, and is intubated. Parents recall a bat bite on her hand 4 months earlier at a cottage, for which she did not seek medical attention. You suspect rabies encephalitis.
questions.question_raw: 4yo girl presenting with right shoulder pain, hypersalivation, etc. symptoms of rabies. She ends up intubated. Parents recall she had a rat (bat in peds) bite on her hand 4 months prior to this at a cottage and did not seek medical attention then. You suspect rabies encephalitis.

parts.text: Name 2 specific diagnostic tests you would do to confirm rabies encephalitis.
Name 2 ways rabies can be transmitted to susceptible humans.
What prophylactic measures could you have done at the time of the bite - describe what and how you would administer them.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 specific diagnostic tests you would do (Adult: to rule out rabies encephalitis) (1)
Name 2 ways rabies can be transmitted to susceptible humans (does not specify it has to be from animals) (1)
What prophylactic measures could you have done at the time of rat (Peds: bat) bite - describe what and how you would administer (2)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) DFA staining / RT-PCR of a full-thickness nuchal skin biopsy (nape of neck, above the hairline, ~10 hair follicles); (2) rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies in serum and CSF (RFFIT), and/or RT-PCR of saliva. b) (1) Bite from a rabid animal with salivary wound contamination; (2) aerosol/mucous-membrane exposure, or organ/corneal transplantation from an infected donor. c) Immediate wound cleansing (20% soap solution +/- povidone-iodine), then HRIG 20 IU/kg with the entire dose infiltrated into/around the wound if anatomically feasible (any remainder IM at a site distant from the vaccine), PLUS rabies vaccine 1.0 mL IM given in the lateral thigh (deltoid in older children/adults, never gluteal) on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 (five doses if immunocompromised).

cohort_answer.text: Diagnostic tests: Full thickness nuchal biopsy looking for Negri bodies; CSF rabies neutralizing antibodies or PCR. Transmission: Bite wound; lab exposure through needlestick, transplant, aerosolization from spelunking/cave exploration. Prophylaxis: RIG injected around bite site and rabies vaccine series starting at same time, doses at 0, 7, 14, 21 days (28 if immunocompromised). DDx furious rabies (80%) if not demonstrating hydrophobia/aerophobia includes other viral encephalitis (HSV), tetanus (opisthotonos can occur in both). DDx paralytic rabies (20%) includes poliomyelitis, transverse myelitis, acute inflammatory polyneuropathy, botulism. Diagnosis: full thickness biopsy from nape of neck above hairline to find virus in cutaneous nerve at base of follicle; multiple specimens/testing methods needed due to limited sensitivity of any one methodology

questions.question: A patient in India is bitten by a macaque and given amoxicillin/clavulanate and a tetanus booster.
questions.question_raw: Q55 (2013 PM). Patient in India is bitten by a macaque and given Amox/Clav and Tetanus booster.

parts.text: What are two fatal infections they are at risk of?
What three agents are indicated?

parts_raw.text: A) What are 2 fatal infections they are at risk of?
B) What 3 agents are indicated?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Herpes B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1) encephalomyelitis (untreated mortality ~70-80%). (2) Rabies.
b) (1) Valacyclovir (1 g PO tid x14d) or acyclovir for herpes B virus postexposure prophylaxis. (2) Rabies immune globulin. (3) Rabies vaccine.
questions.beyond_mandell: Rabies risk and rabies PEP (RIG + vaccine) are not from this chapter; per WHO/CDC rabies postexposure prophylaxis for a macaque bite in a rabies-endemic region.

cohort_answer.text:
Herpes B virus; Rabies
Rabies Ig and vaccine; Acyclovir, B virus specific Ig if available

parts_raw.text: Herpes B

questions.model_answer: a) Herpes B (Macacine herpesvirus 1): macaque monkeys (Old World macaques, e.g. rhesus and cynomolgus). b) Sin Nombre virus: the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. c) Rabies: mammalian reservoirs vary by region—in North America, bats plus terrestrial carnivores (raccoons, skunks, foxes); worldwide the dog is the dominant reservoir. d) Chlamydia psittaci: psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets, cockatiels) and other birds.

cohort_answer.text: Herpes B: Macaque monkey. Sin Nombre virus: Deer mouse/rat. Rabies: Bats and raccoons. Chlamydia psittaci: Parrots.
